cmo-cjmo-2025-01.title: Expand $(1+kd)^3$
cmo-cjmo-2025-01.body:
Let the progression be $a, a+d, a+2d, \ldots$ with integers $a$ and $d \ne 0$ (non-constant). Since $1$ is a term, $1 = a + jd$ for some $j \ge 0$, and then the terms $a + (j+m)d = 1 + md$ show that **every number $1 + md$ with $m$ a non-negative integer is in the progression.**

For a positive integer $k$,
$$(1+kd)^3 = 1 + 3kd + 3k^2d^2 + k^3d^3 = 1 + d\cdot m_k, \qquad m_k = k\,(3 + 3kd + k^2d^2).$$
For every real $t$ we have $t^2 + 3t + 3 = \left(t + \tfrac32\right)^2 + \tfrac34 > 0$; with $t = kd$ this shows that $m_k$ is a **positive** integer (whatever the sign of $d$). Hence $(1+kd)^3 = 1 + m_k d$ is a term of the progression for every $k = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$

Finally, the integers $1 + kd$ ($k = 1, 2, \ldots$) are pairwise different because $d \ne 0$, and $x \mapsto x^3$ is injective on the integers, so these are infinitely many different perfect cubes. ∎

cmo-cjmo-2025-01.title: Work modulo $|d|$
cmo-cjmo-2025-01.body:
As above, the progression contains all numbers $1 + md$ with $m \ge 0$. Put $e = |d| \ge 1$.

- If $d > 0$: every integer $x \ge 1$ with $x \equiv 1 \pmod e$ is of the form $1 + md$ with $m \ge 0$, so it is a term.
- If $d < 0$: every integer $x \le 1$ with $x \equiv 1 \pmod e$ is of the form $1 + md$ with $m \ge 0$, so it is a term.

Now take $k = 1 + se$ with $s = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ if $d > 0$, and $k = 1 - se$ with $s = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ if $d < 0$. Then $k \equiv 1 \pmod e$, so $k^3 \equiv 1 \pmod e$; and $k^3 \ge 1$ in the first case, $k^3 \le 1$ in the second. So each $k^3$ is a term, and they are pairwise different. Hence the progression contains infinitely many perfect cubes. ∎

cmo-cjmo-2025-02.title: Two new cyclic quadrilaterals and the radical center
cmo-cjmo-2025-02.body:
Let $\omega$ be the given circle. For points $U, V$ on a line through $T$ write $TU\cdot TV$ for the **signed** product (positive when $U, V$ are on the same side of $T$). We use the power of a point: if a line through $T$ meets a circle at $U, V$, then $TU \cdot TV$ is the power of $T$ with respect to that circle; and its converse: if two different lines through $T$ contain $U, V$ and $U', V'$ (all different from $T$) with $TU\cdot TV = TU'\cdot TV'$, then $U, V, U', V'$ are concyclic.

If the legs $AD$ and $BC$ were parallel, $ABCD$ would be a parallelogram and $BC = DA$; so the lines $AD$ and $BC$ meet at a point $O$. Let $P$ be the intersection of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$.

**Step 1: $A, B, Y, X$ are concyclic.** Because $AB \parallel DC$, the homothety with centre $O$ that maps $D$ to $A$ maps $C$ to $B$: with the same factor $\lambda$, $\overrightarrow{OA} = \lambda\overrightarrow{OD}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB} = \lambda\overrightarrow{OC}$. The line $AD$ meets $\omega$ at $D, X$ and the line $BC$ meets $\omega$ at $C, Y$, so $OD\cdot OX = OC \cdot OY$ (both equal the power of $O$). Multiplying by $\lambda$:
$$OA \cdot OX = OB \cdot OY,$$
so $A, X, B, Y$ lie on a circle $\omega_1$.

**Step 2: $A, B, Z, W$ are concyclic.** Similarly the homothety with centre $P$ mapping $C$ to $A$ maps $D$ to $B$ (factor $\mu < 0$). The line $AC$ meets $\omega$ at $C, W$ and $BD$ meets $\omega$ at $D, Z$, so $PC \cdot PW = PD\cdot PZ$, and multiplying by $\mu$ gives $PA\cdot PW = PB \cdot PZ$. So $A, W, B, Z$ lie on a circle $\omega_2$.

**Step 3: $XY$ is not parallel to $AB$.** Suppose $XY \parallel AB \parallel DC$. Then $\overrightarrow{OX} = t\,\overrightarrow{OD}$ and $\overrightarrow{OY} = t\,\overrightarrow{OC}$ for some $t \ne 0$ ($t = 0$ would give $X = Y = O$). Then $OD \cdot OX = OC \cdot OY$ becomes $t\,OD^2 = t\,OC^2$, so $OD = OC$, hence $OA = |\lambda| OD = OB$, and $DA = |1-\lambda|\,OD = |1 - \lambda|\,OC = CB$, contradicting $BC \ne DA$.

**Step 4: radical axes.** The radical axis of two circles meeting at two points is the line through them. So
- line $AB$ is the radical axis of $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$,
- line $XY$ is the radical axis of $\omega$ and $\omega_1$,
- line $WZ$ is the radical axis of $\omega$ and $\omega_2$.

By Step 3, the lines $AB$ and $XY$ meet at a point $K$. Then $K$ has the same power with respect to $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ (it is on $AB$) and the same power with respect to $\omega$ and $\omega_1$ (it is on $XY$), so it has the same power with respect to $\omega$ and $\omega_2$, i.e. $K$ lies on their radical axis $WZ$. Hence $WZ$, $XY$, $AB$ all pass through $K$. ∎

cmo-cjmo-2025-03.title: Shrink the cycle, then shrink the paths
cmo-cjmo-2025-03.body:
Write $f(a)$ for the player $a$ currently votes for, and draw an arrow $a \to f(a)$. An update of $a$ replaces $f(a)$ by $f(f(a))$. For $n = 1$ there is nothing to prove, so let $n \ge 2$.

**1. There is always exactly one cycle, and the set of players on it only shrinks.** The graph starts as one $n$-cycle, so it is (weakly) connected. When $a$ with $a \to b \to c$ switches to $a \to c$, the edge $b \to c$ is still there, so $a$ stays connected to $b$: the graph stays connected. A connected graph in which every vertex has exactly one outgoing arrow has exactly one cycle. If $a$ is not on the cycle, its update does not touch the cycle's arrows, so the cycle is unchanged. If $a$ is on the cycle and the cycle has length $K \ge 2$, then $b \ne a$ and $c$ are the next two cycle vertices (with $c = a$ if $K = 2$); after the update the cycle is the old one with $b$ skipped, of length $K - 1$. If the cycle is a self-loop $a \to a$, nothing changes. So the set of cycle vertices never gains a vertex, and each update by a cycle vertex while the cycle has length $\ge 2$ removes exactly one vertex from it.

**2. In each round the cycle length $K \ge 2$ drops to at most $\lfloor K/2 \rfloor$.** Let $s$ be the cycle length at the end of the round. If $s = 1$ this is clear. If $s \ge 2$, the cycle had length $\ge 2$ during the whole round, and each of the $s$ final cycle vertices was on the cycle during the whole round (vertices never rejoin), so each of their $s$ updates removed a vertex from the cycle; removed vertices never return, so these are $s$ different vertices. Hence $K - s \ge s$, i.e. $s \le \lfloor K/2\rfloor$.

Since $\lfloor\lfloor x/2\rfloor/2\rfloor = \lfloor x/4\rfloor$ etc., after $r$ rounds the cycle has length at most $\max(1, \lfloor n/2^r\rfloor)$, which equals $1$ for $r = m := \lfloor \log_2 n\rfloor$ (as $2^{m+1} > n$). So after $m$ rounds the cycle is a self-loop at some player $z$, and by step 1 it stays so forever ($z$'s update gives $f(z) = f(f(z)) = z$).

**3. Afterwards the depths halve.** Once $z \to z$ is the only cycle, every player $a$ reaches $z$ by following arrows; let the *depth* $h(a)$ be the number of arrows needed ($h(z) = 0$). An update never increases depths: if $h(a) \ge 2$ the update moves $a$ one step closer (decreasing $h(a)$ and the depths of players whose path passes through $a$ by $1$), and if $h(a) \le 1$ nothing changes.

*Claim.* In any round (after step 2 is completed), each player $a$ with depth $h$ at the start of the round has depth at most $\lceil h/2\rceil$ at the end of the round.

*Proof by strong induction on $h$.* For $h \le 1$ it holds since depths do not increase. Let $h \ge 2$ and let $a \to b \to c$ at the start of the round, so $b$ and $c$ have starting depths $h-1$ and $h-2$. Each player updates exactly once per round, so until $a$'s update $a$ still points to $b$, and after it $a$'s arrow is fixed for the rest of the round.
- If $b$ has not updated yet when $a$ updates, $b$ still points to $c$ and $a$ switches to $c$ for the rest of the round. So $a$'s final depth is $1 + (\text{final depth of } c) \le 1 + \lceil (h-2)/2\rceil = \lceil h/2\rceil$ by the induction hypothesis.
- If $b$ updated earlier, $b$ already points to its final target $e$, and $a$ switches to $e$. Then $a$ and $b$ both point to $e$ at the end, so they have the same final depth, which is $\le \lceil (h-1)/2 \rceil \le \lceil h/2\rceil$ by the induction hypothesis applied to $b$. $\square$

When the self-loop appears, every depth is at most $n - 1$ (a path in an $n$-vertex graph). After $r$ further rounds every depth is at most $\lceil (n-1)/2^r\rceil$, which is $\le 1$ once $2^r \ge n - 1$, i.e. after $r = \lceil \log_2 (n-1)\rceil$ rounds. Depth $\le 1$ for everyone means everyone votes for $z$, and this stays true in later rounds (all updates then change nothing).

**4. Counting rounds.** We need $m + \lceil \log_2(n-1)\rceil \le n$ where $2^m \le n < 2^{m+1}$. Since $n - 1 < 2^{m+1}$, the total is at most $2m + 1$.
- $m \ge 3$: $2m + 1 \le 2^m \le n$ (true for $m = 3$ and the left side grows by $2$ while the right side at least doubles).
- $m = 2$ ($4 \le n \le 7$): $n = 4$ gives $2 + \lceil\log_2 3\rceil = 4 \le 4$; $n \ge 5$ gives total $\le 5 \le n$.
- $m = 1$ ($n = 2, 3$): totals $1 + 0 = 1 \le 2$ and $1 + 1 = 2 \le 3$.

So after $n$ rounds, all players vote for $z$. ∎

cmo-cjmo-2025-04.title: Factor and use powers of 2 and 3
cmo-cjmo-2025-04.body:
**Step 1: $p = 3$.** Factor the right side:
$$2^a p^b = (p+2)^c - 1 = (p+1)\left((p+2)^{c-1} + \cdots + (p+2) + 1\right).$$
So $p + 1$ divides $2^a p^b$. As $\gcd(p+1, p) = 1$, $p + 1$ divides $2^a$, so $p + 1 = 2^x$ is a power of $2$. Among the three consecutive integers $p, p+1, p+2$ one is divisible by $3$; it is not $p + 1 = 2^x$, so $3 \mid p$ or $3 \mid p+2$. Both are primes, so $p = 3$ or $p + 2 = 3$; the latter gives $p = 1$, not a prime. Hence $p = 3$ (and indeed $p + 2 = 5$ is prime).

**Step 2: $c$ is even.** Now $2^a 3^b = 5^c - 1$ with $b \ge 1$, so $5^c \equiv 1 \pmod 3$. As $5 \equiv -1 \pmod 3$, $(-1)^c \equiv 1$, so $c = 2d$ with $d \ge 1$, and
$$2^a 3^b = (5^d - 1)(5^d + 1).$$

**Step 3: $d = 1$.** The two factors are even and differ by $2$, so their gcd is $2$; in particular $3$ divides at most one of them. If $3 \mid 5^d - 1$, then $5^d + 1$ has no factor $3$, so it is a power of $2$; but $5^d + 1 \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, so $5^d + 1 = 2$, impossible. Hence $3 \nmid 5^d - 1$ and $5^d - 1$ is a power of $2$. Now $3 \nmid 5^d - 1$ means $(-1)^d \not\equiv 1 \pmod 3$, so $d$ is odd. Then
$$5^d - 1 = 4\cdot\left(5^{d-1} + 5^{d-2} + \cdots + 1\right),$$
and the bracket is a sum of $d$ odd numbers, hence odd; being a factor of a power of $2$ it equals $1$, which forces $d = 1$.

**Step 4.** So $c = 2$ and $2^a 3^b = 24 = 2^3\cdot 3$, giving $a = 3$, $b = 1$. Check: $2^3\cdot 3^1 = 24 = 5^2 - 1$.

**Answer: $(a, b, c, p) = (3, 1, 2, 3)$ only.**

cmo-cjmo-2025-05.title: Explicit formulas with reversed polynomials
cmo-cjmo-2025-05.body:
**Reformulating reflexivity.** For a polynomial $a(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{d} c_i x^i$ of degree $d$ and an integer $N \ge d$, the coefficient of $x^j$ in $x^N a(1/x) = \sum_i c_i x^{N-i}$ is $c_{N-j}$ (with $c_i = 0$ for $i > d$). Hence $a$ is reflexive iff $a(x) = x^N a(1/x)$ for some integer $N \ge \deg a$. (The zero polynomial is reflexive trivially.)

**The construction.** Let $d = \deg p$ (if $p = 0$ take $q = r = 0$), fix an integer $m \ge \max(d, 1)$ and put $P_N(x) = x^N p(1/x)$ for $N \ge d$; this is a polynomial with integer coefficients, of degree at most $N$, with $P_N(1) = p(1)$ and $x^\ell P_m(x) = P_{m+\ell}(x)$. Define
$$q(x) = \frac{P_{m+\ell}(x) - p(x)}{x - 1}, \qquad r(x) = \frac{p(x) - P_m(x)}{x - 1}.$$

**They are integer polynomials.** Each numerator is an integer polynomial vanishing at $x = 1$, so it is divisible by $x - 1$; since $x - 1$ is monic, the quotient has integer coefficients. Also $\deg q \le m + \ell - 1$ and $\deg r \le m - 1$ (numerators have degree $\le m + \ell$, resp. $\le m$).

**The identity.**
$$q(x) + x^\ell r(x) = \frac{P_{m+\ell} - p + x^\ell p - x^\ell P_m}{x - 1} = \frac{(x^\ell - 1)\,p(x)}{x-1} = (1 + x + \cdots + x^{\ell-1})\,p(x).$$

**$q$ is reflexive** (with $N = m + \ell - 1 \ge \deg q$):
$$x^{m+\ell-1} q(1/x) = x^{m+\ell-1}\cdot\frac{x^{-(m+\ell)}p(x) - p(1/x)}{1/x - 1} = \frac{p(x) - x^{m+\ell}p(1/x)}{1 - x} = \frac{P_{m+\ell}(x) - p(x)}{x - 1} = q(x).$$

**$r$ is reflexive** (with $N = m - 1 \ge \deg r$; note $m \ge 1$):
$$x^{m-1} r(1/x) = x^{m-1}\cdot\frac{p(1/x) - x^{-m}p(x)}{1/x - 1} = \frac{x^m p(1/x) - p(x)}{1 - x} = \frac{p(x) - P_m(x)}{x - 1} = r(x).$$

So $q$ and $r$ are reflexive integer polynomials with $(1 + x + \cdots + x^{\ell - 1})p(x) = q(x) + x^\ell r(x)$. ∎

*Example.* $p(x) = 1 + 2x$, $\ell = 2$, $m = 1$: $P_1 = x + 2$, $P_3 = x^3 + 2x^2$, so $q = \frac{x^3 + 2x^2 - 2x - 1}{x - 1} = x^2 + 3x + 1$ and $r = \frac{1 + 2x - x - 2}{x - 1} = 1$; indeed $(1 + x)(1 + 2x) = 1 + 3x + 2x^2 = (x^2 + 3x + 1) + x^2\cdot 1$.
